To: Jaya, Customer Support
Subject: Help after data leak

Dear Jaya,

I'm writing because I did the wrong thing. On 4 February your company sent an email saying some customer details had leaked. It looked like junk, so I deleted it without reading past the first line.

Six weeks later I began getting calls from people who knew my name and the address I gave you, saying they were from my delivery service. I lost a whole afternoon and gave one of them a code before I realised something was off.

Could you tell me what exactly was in the leak, and whether anything can still be done? I know I waited too long.

Mohit

Reply: "We're sorry. We will help, though the delay does make tracing harder."

qa.q: On what date did the company send the notice?
What was Mohit feeling when writing that the wrong thing was done?
qa.a: Mohit felt regret and worry, blaming the delay in reading the notice and realising too late that the calls were a trick.

qa.q: What could Mohit do now besides asking the company, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could tell the bank and keep a record of the calls, because reporting quickly and keeping details helps others trace what happened.

qa.q: How might Jaya see Mohit's email?
qa.a: Jaya may see a customer who is embarrassed but honest, and would want to help while knowing the six-week gap limits what can be traced.

grounding: The user assumes the breach email is junk and deletes it, then weeks later phishing calls use the leaked details, and the delay makes tracing harder.

Gopika, you know those calls I've been getting? I finally know why, and it's my own fault. I'm Hafsa, and I delete everything.
In June an email came from the travel-booking site I use, subject line 'Important security notice'. I thought, obviously spam, and deleted it without opening it. I get twenty of those a week.
In July the calls started. A man who knew my full name, my phone number and the Goa trip I booked in April. He said he was from the site, my refund was stuck, and he needed the OTP to 'release it'. I nearly gave it. Something in his voice made me hang up.
Then I searched and found the breach had been in the news. My details were in it. When I called the real company, they said they'd sent me a notice in June with steps to take. And now, because it's been weeks, the bank says it's much harder to trace where the calls come from.
So I read the security emails now, Gopika. Every one. Carefully.

qa.q: What did the caller ask Hafsa for?
How does Hafsa feel now that the reason for the calls is clear?
qa.a: Frustrated and shaken, realising that deleting the notice left Hafsa open to the calls.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done when the notice arrived in June?
qa.a: Opened it, checked it came from the real company, and followed its steps, such as watching for calls that quote the Goa booking.

qa.q: What might Gopika take from Hafsa's story?
qa.a: Gopika may start reading such emails carefully too, having heard how close Hafsa came to sharing an OTP.

grounding: Shows a user deleting a breach notice as spam, then facing phishing calls weeks later that are harder to trace because of the delay.

I'm Santosh, Zubin's flatmate, and I was there when he deleted it. It was a Sunday morning in March. He was clearing his inbox, and I saw the subject line go past, something like 'Notice of data incident', from the online bookstore he uses. He laughed, said, 'Nice try, spammers,' and deleted it.
About a month later he started getting texts: 'Your order is on hold, click to verify your address.' They used his real name and the exact title of a book he had ordered. He showed me one, puzzled. 'How do they know about this book?'
Only when he searched the bookstore's name did he find the breach, and the notice he had deleted. The bookstore's helpline confirmed his name, address, phone and order history were in it. He filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal that day, but was told that after a month the numbers sending the texts had already changed.
He went quiet for a bit. Then he set up a filter so security notices go to a folder he checks every week.

qa.q: What did Zubin say when he deleted the email?
How did Zubin seem to feel when the texts mentioned his book?
qa.a: Puzzled and uneasy, not understanding how strangers knew about his order.

qa.q: What did Zubin change afterwards, and why does it help?
qa.a: A filter sending security notices to a folder checked weekly, so real notices are read before damage builds.

qa.q: How does the whole episode look to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh saw the notice deleted in a moment, then watched the consequences build, noticing Zubin go quiet.

grounding: Shows a user deleting a breach notice as junk and later receiving phishing texts that are harder to trace after the delay.
